newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Senate committee passes tax cut bill.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Senate committee passes tax cut bill.

text.p: The Senate Finance Committee approved tax cut legislation late Thursday that included last-minute changes to reduce an airline tax and increase the cigarette tax.
The committee voted 18-2 for the revised bill after meeting for hours behind closed doors to hammer out the changes. Two Republicans voted against the revised plan.

"That in one day we were able to reach agreement and pass this legislation almost unanimously, I think it speaks for the good will of the committee members," Senate Finance Committee Chairman William Roth, a Delaware Republican, said. The vote showed "strong bipartisan support," he said.

Tax legislation passed the House Ways and Means Committee last week without any Democrats voting for it. The tax bill is needed to implement a budget agreement reached between congressional leaders and the White House last month that called for $85 billion in net tax cuts over five years.
"Basically our legislation meets the requirements of the budget," Roth said. The Senate committee did not have final figures on how the late changes affected the overall tax cut.
Sen. Daniel Patrick Moynihan, the committee's senior Democrat, called the outcome "solid."

The Senate bill would increase the federal cigarette tax by about 20 cents per pack from the current 24 cents, to raise about $15 billion over five years. House tax legislation does not contain a cigarette tax increase.

The initial airline tax proposal to impose a 10 percent tax on the portion of an international ticket that represented flight in U.S. airspace was scrapped. It was replaced by a 10 percent tax on domestic segments of international flights and an $8 departure and arrival tax. Currently there is a $6 departure tax.
The new airline proposal would raise about $3.5 billion over five years, about half the revenues that would have come from the original plan.

Sen. Phil Gramm, a Texas Republican, early in the day likened the original international ticket tax proposal to "putting a cover charge at a department store," saying it discouraged tourism to the United States.
However, Gramm was one of the two votes against the revised legislation, saying "a late tax increase and spending increase sank the tax cut in terms of my voting for it."
Differences between Senate and House legislation must be worked out before a tax bill can be sent to the president. The House and Senate are expected to vote on their respective tax bills next week.
Other changes in the Senate legislation partly addressed concerns expressed by the Clinton administration.

Families who receive the earned income tax credit for the working poor would be able to get more of the $500-per-child tax credit. The Clinton administration is pushing for the child tax credit to go to low-income familes who don't owe taxes, so in essence the government would give them money.
The new bill would raise the threshold at which the inheritance tax kicks in to $1 million in 2007 from the current $600,000, a year earlier than the initial plan.
The committee approved an amendment that would extend tax breaks for ethanol producers but at the same time gradually reduce that subsidy over five years.
A small change would allow Individual Retirement Accounts to invest in gold bullion.

The committee voted to add another $8 billion over five years to the $16 billion it approved earlier this week to deliver health care to uninsured children through an expansion of the Medicaid programme.

The tax legislation included tax credits for college tuition and a capital gains tax rate cut to 20 percent from a maximum 28 percent for individuals. It would also allow married couples to exclude from taxes up to $500,000 of gain from selling a home.
